prompt.context: Our client is a company which is going to exploit a mine that is expected to be full of a very unique ore, and has asked us in which order his company should extract the ore from the field. The ore will then be sent to a factory that his company already owns.
prompt.question: In what order should the client extract ore cells from the mine field in order to maximize profits?

clarifying_info.a: The field is divided into cells of equal size. Once you blow (extract) one cell, a truck cannot pass through it to reach the factory.

clarifying_info.q: Are the cells uniform in ore content?
clarifying_info.a: No. Each cell has different ore content and therefore each cell has a different cost of extraction.
The factory processes rocks containing 1% ore and outputs 100% ore. Trucks enter the factory with the ore-bearing rocks.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current price of ore?
clarifying_info.a: The client expects to get $10 per ton of ore.

clarifying_info.q: Are the extraction costs fixed or variable?
clarifying_info.a: The costs appear to be fixed and do not change with overall price fluctuations.

exhibits.title: Mine Field Map with Cell Data
exhibits.shows: A grid map of the mine field showing the factory location and three labeled cells, each with its ore content (x, in tons) and extraction cost (C, in dollars).
exhibits.data: Cell 1: x=1.0 tons, C=$3; Cell 2: x=1.3 tons, C=$10; Cell 3: x=1.1 tons, C=$5; Factory shown at bottom-right; cells arranged so extracted cells block truck routes to the factory

framework: Profitability per cell: rank cells by (price per ton * ore content) minus extraction cost
Demand / price outlook: consider whether ore price is expected to rise; if so, extracting lower-concentration cells first at low prices may be optimal
Plant capacity constraints: identify minimum and maximum throughput requirements and any penalties for operating outside that range
Operational / routing constraints: blowing a cell removes that route; start extraction from cells furthest from the factory to avoid blocking access to remaining cells
Break-even and P&L analysis: understand fixed vs. variable cost structure to determine how volume affects profitability

questions.prompt: At a price of $10/ton, in what order should the client extract Cell 1, Cell 2, and Cell 3?
questions.guidance: Candidate should define profit as (price * ore content) - extraction cost, calculate per cell, and rank descending. Should also note that blocking a cell blocks truck routes.

math.setup: Profit per cell = (price per ton) * (tons of ore in cell) - (extraction cost). Price = $10/ton.
math.answer: Extraction order at $10/ton: Cell 1 (profit $7), then Cell 3 (profit $6), then Cell 2 (profit $3).

questions.prompt: If the price rises to $30/ton, does the extraction order change? Why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate profits at the new price. Higher ore-content cells benefit disproportionately from a price increase, changing the relative ranking. Candidate should note extraction costs are fixed.

math.setup: Profit per cell = (price per ton) * (tons of ore in cell) - (extraction cost). Price = $30/ton.
math.answer: Extraction order at $30/ton: Cell 2 (profit $29), then Cell 3 (profit $28), then Cell 1 (profit $27). Yes, the order changes because cells with higher ore content benefit more from a higher price, while costs remain fixed.

questions.prompt: Given the following per-ton P&L (Revenue $1.0, COGS $0.8, SG&A $0.6, Profit -$0.4), what is the company's break-even point? How does the P&L look at break-even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify gross margin, then divide fixed SG&A by gross margin to find the break-even multiplier. Should note that SG&A must remain fixed (not scale with volume) for this analysis to hold.

math.setup: Gross margin = Revenue - COGS = $1.0 - $0.8 = $0.2 per ton. Break-even multiplier = SG&A / Gross margin.
steps: P&L at break-even: Revenue $1.0, COGS $0.8, SG&A $0.2, Profit $0.0
math.answer: The company must produce 3 times its current volume to cover fixed SG&A costs. At that volume, the per-ton P&L is: Revenue $1.0, COGS $0.8, SG&A $0.2, Profit $0.0.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors besides current profit should influence the extraction order?

categories.name: Price / Demand Outlook
ideas: If ore price is expected to rise, extract lower-concentration (lower-profit) cells first while price is low
Store ore if storage cost and opportunity cost are acceptable; otherwise extract in anticipation of higher prices
Model price scenarios (base, upside, downside) before committing to extraction sequence

categories.name: Plant Capacity Constraints
ideas: Identify minimum throughput required to keep the factory running efficiently
Identify maximum throughput the factory can handle
Assess penalties for operating outside the min-max range
Plan extraction rate to match plant capacity

categories.name: Operational / Routing Constraints
ideas: Map all possible truck routes from each cell to the factory before extraction begins
Extract cells furthest from the factory first to preserve route optionality
Identify bottleneck cells whose extraction would block access to multiple other cells
Model the sequence as a graph problem: cells are nodes, truck paths are edges

categories.name: Financial / Cost Considerations
ideas: Opportunity cost of tying up capital in unexploited ore
Fixed vs. variable cost structure and its impact on volume targets
SG&A leverage: higher volume spreads fixed costs and improves margins
Financing costs of mine development and equipment

categories.name: Strategic / Market Factors
ideas: Competitor behavior and market supply dynamics
Regulatory or environmental permits that may restrict extraction timing
Contract obligations requiring minimum delivery volumes
Optionality value of leaving high-ore cells for later if prices are expected to rise significantly

recommendation: At the current price of $10/ton, extract cells in descending profit order: Cell 1 first ($7 profit), Cell 3 second ($6), Cell 2 last ($3), while always preserving truck routes to the factory
Increase extraction volume to at least 3x current levels to reach break-even and cover fixed SG&A costs
risks: Ore price volatility can invert the optimal extraction sequence; a price rise to $30/ton changes order to Cell 2, Cell 3, Cell 1
Extracting a cell that blocks access to remaining cells destroys option value and reduces total recoverable profit
If SG&A scales with volume, the break-even multiplier would be higher than 3x
Demand outlook uncertainty makes it difficult to optimize the sequence without price forecasts
next_steps: Map all truck routes before any extraction to identify which cell sequences preserve full access to the field
Build a price scenario model to stress-test extraction sequencing under different ore price assumptions
Confirm whether SG&A costs are truly fixed or partially variable at higher extraction volumes
Determine plant capacity constraints (min/max throughput) and align extraction schedule accordingly
